summary: Describes a Vendor-Specific LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF), allowing organizations to use implementation-specific encodings for LCAF addresses. It updates RFC 8060. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9306 adds a LISP address format for encodings defined by a particular organization. It also says how LISP control messages handle unknown address-format types.

questions: how can vendors define custom lisp address formats
what happens to unrecognized lcaf types
what is an oui in lisp
subtitle: A LISP address format for organization-defined encodings.

tldr.problem: Some LISP deployments need address encodings that are specific to an organization or implementation, and RFC 8060 did not specify how to handle unknown LCAF types.
tldr.mechanism: The Vendor-Specific LCAF uses type 255, an IEEE-assigned 24-bit OUI, and an organization-defined internal format. Unknown types must be ignored.
tldr.outcome: The format is intended for implementation-specific use and should not be used where organizations need to interoperate. RFC 9306 updates RFC 8060.

today: RFC 9306 is Experimental and updates RFC 8060. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces RFC 9306.

sections.title: Why Add a Vendor-Specific Format
sections.content:
The LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF), defined in RFC 8060, describes encodings for address types used by the Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP). Some deployments need encodings that apply only to a particular use case.

RFC 9306 adds a Vendor-Specific LCAF for organization-defined formats and updates RFC 8060 with rules for unrecognized LCAF types.
sections.plainLanguage: An organization can define its own LISP address encoding for a specific deployment. The RFC also sets rules for address types a device does not recognize.

sections.title: Handling Unknown LCAF Types
sections.content:
A LISP control-plane message containing an unrecognized LCAF type MUST have that type ignored. If all locators are ignored, the result is equivalent to a control message with Locator Count = 0.

If an EID-Prefix contains only unrecognized LCAF types, the control message MUST be dropped and the event MUST be logged. EID means Endpoint Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A device skips an address type it does not understand. If an EID-Prefix contains only unknown types, the device drops the whole control message and records the event.

sections.title: Fields in the Vendor-Specific LCAF
sections.content:
The format begins with the general LCAF fields. Its AFI is 16387, its Type is 255, and its Length covers the internal format, the OUI, and Rsvd3.

Rsvd3 is an 8-bit reserved field that MUST be zero when sent and ignored when received. The 24-bit OUI is assigned by the IEEE Registration Authority. The remaining internal format has variable length and is left for each vendor or organization to define.
sections.plainLanguage: The type value identifies this as vendor-specific. An IEEE-assigned organization identifier distinguishes the owner, followed by data that the organization defines.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says this LCAF type SHOULD NOT be used in deployments where different organizations interoperate. Organizations that explicitly agree to share a deployment need to assess its interoperability. Using an OUI not assigned to the organization is NOT RECOMMENDED.

A LISP device that does not understand the OUI MUST drop the message and SHOULD log it. Each organization is responsible for assessing the security implications of its own internal format; the security considerations in RFC 8060 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Because each organization defines its own internal format, other organizations may not understand it. Organizations must assess the compatibility and security of formats they choose to share.
